entries.title: Funding and budget qualifying questions
entries.summary: Questions that surface the prospect's funding process, budget range, approval obstacles, and other decision-makers, plus scripts for when the prospect claims they have no money, guiding them to find the funds themselves.

questions: Could you walk me through how you fund or budget for solving problems like this?
Just so I know how I can help, what budget or funding range are you working within?
How will the funding for this project actually get decided?
What roadblocks might come up when you go to get financial sign-off to solve [the problem]?
Besides you, who else would need to approve the funding to fix this?
How would you go about getting the company to approve funding for [the issue] you described?
What kind of budget are you able to put toward this so you can get started on [what they wanted]?
If you did have the funding in place, is this something that would work for you?
I get that budget might be tight based on what you shared. How do you think you could work that out so you can free up the funds to [what they wanted]?
What other avenues could you tap to find the funds so you can [what they wanted]?

Can I offer a suggestion? I can walk you through the routes other clients used to free up funds when they did not have them on hand, and you can see which are open to you. Which of those could work for you, so you can solve [the problem]?

entries.trigger_signal: stage=qualify AND budget/funding not yet established OR prospect raises a money concern

entries.title: Proposal process rules and three-option structure
entries.summary: Rules for proposals: never send one before understanding the problem and budget, restate the prospect's problems and objectives to revive pain and desired outcomes, keep value at least 10x price, always give three price tiers, and make the proposal a signable agreement.

points: Never send a proposal before you understand the prospect's problems and whether they have the budget to solve them, no exceptions, even if they ask for just pricing early.
A proposal should restate the two or three problems and two or three objectives the prospect shared, to revive the pain and the desired outcome and prove you understood their situation.
Aim for the value of solving their problems to be at least ten times the price of your offer, so the cost feels small next to the payoff.

Offer three options every time: a lower-priced but still profitable basic tier, a middle core offering where most prospects land, and a premium high-priced tier. The premium anchor makes the middle option feel like a bargain and lifts both close rate and deal size.

Make the proposal double as a simple signable agreement so buying is one easy step. Every extra step and delay raises the odds the deal falls apart; treat the signature as a micro-commitment that leads to the full commitment.

entries.trigger_signal: stage=commit AND rep is about to build or send a proposal or pricing

entries.title: Deflecting a premature proposal request
entries.summary: A response for when a prospect asks for a proposal or pricing before discovery is done, redirecting them back to a few situation questions so anything you send is actually useful.

questions: I am glad to put a proposal together for you. Honestly though, I am not sure yet that we are even the right fit. It would probably serve you better if we ran through a few questions about your situation first, then built something that is actually useful. Would that be okay with you?

entries.trigger_signal: prospect requests a proposal or pricing before discovery is complete

entries.title: Qualifying questions and hypothetical templates
entries.summary: Questions that gauge how important and urgent solving the problem is, plus hypothetical opener and closer phrase banks and a travel-or-demo qualifier that confirms commitment before you invest significant selling time.

questions: How important is solving this to you? (curious, lightly skeptical tone)
How important is it for you to change your situation and get to [what they want]?
How important is it that you do something about this, and why now?
Is fixing this problem actually important to you, and why?
If you could, what would that do for you?
Are you ready to change your situation so you can [what they want]?
It sounds like [what they are frustrated with] really bothers you. So if you could get what you want, how important is it to make that happen, and why now?

Say I did come out for a full day, you got the owners and other decision-makers in the room, and everyone agreed we can solve [the problems they mentioned] the way we do for other clients. What do you see happening next?
Let's say we could solve [their problem]. What do you feel would happen next?
Suppose we pulled this off for you. Where would we go from there?
Imagine for a second we got you [what you want]. What would you want to happen next?
Assuming we managed to fix this. What do you see happening from there?

entries.trigger_signal: stage=qualify AND urgency or commitment not yet confirmed

entries.title: Reading urgency and obstacles from qualifying responses
entries.summary: How to interpret a prospect's answer to a hypothetical qualifying question to gauge urgency, surface hidden decision-makers or budget gaps, and decide whether to invest significant selling time.

points: A prospect's answer to a hypothetical qualifying question reveals where the deal really stands and how much urgency exists.
We would definitely move forward means a green light that is worth investing your time and travel.
We would have to run it past a committee or corporate means there are hidden decision-makers to uncover.
We would need to secure budget means the funding is not yet in place.
We would have to compare it to our current provider means the incumbent is still in play.
I am not sure what would happen means there is not enough urgency or trust yet.
Only invest significant selling time such as travel or in-person demos after securing smaller commitments; if the answer is anything but a clear green light, remove those obstacles first.
Listen for what the prospect means, not just their literal words; read tonality and body language for true urgency.

entries.trigger_signal: stage=qualify AND rep is interpreting a prospect response or deciding whether to invest time

entries.title: Handling a send-me-references request
entries.summary: A reference request is almost always a hidden concern. Uncover the real concern, lock in a next-step commitment, and pre-close on the outcome so the prospect does not use references as a way to disappear.

questions: Absolutely, I can do that. So I connect you with the right person, what specifically would you want to dig into with them? (surfaces the real concern)
Makes sense. When are you planning to reach out to them, so I can give them a heads-up and make sure they are available for you? (locks a commitment)
Let's say the references confirm we solved the same kind of problem you are dealing with. Where do you feel we would go from there? (pre-close on the outcome)

entries.trigger_signal: prospect asks for references or testimonials

entries.title: Redirect a 'just send me something' stall into discovery
entries.summary: When a prospect tries to end the call early by asking you to email info or a proposal, agree, then use questions to reframe the stall back into a discovery conversation before committing to send anything.

questions: Absolutely - what are you hoping the proposal will actually show you?
Before I put anything together, would it make sense for me to first understand what you're doing today around X? You might not even need us - so, for instance, what are you currently using for...?
Let's assume I get you that proposal and we're able to solve the X issues you raised so you can reach the outcome you mentioned - what would you see as the next step from there?
Happy to send that over - so I send you the right thing, what exactly are you hoping to see?
And who or what are you using for that right now?

That's a helpful start. What I can do, if you'd like, is send over how we might solve the X problems you mentioned. Once you and your team have looked it over to see whether it fits - what would you want the next step to be?

entries.trigger_signal: prospect issues an early stall such as 'just send me a proposal/quote' or 'email me some info and I'll get back to you' before any gap/problem has been built

entries.title: Turn 'call me back, I'm too busy' into a booked time
entries.summary: When a prospect stalls with 'call me back later,' avoid the endless chase by either handing them your number and asking their timeframe (positioning you as busy), or booking a specific calendar slot together.

questions: No problem. I'll give you my number and you can call me back later today to catch me - would that help? My number is X. What's your timeframe for getting back to me today, just so I know whether I'll be free for you?

It can be tough to catch me at random with my schedule. Here's an idea: if you've got your calendar handy, I'll grab mine and we'll lock in a specific time - that way neither of us has to chase the other down. Would that work for you?
If you have your calendar in front of you, I can pull mine up and we'll book a set time so nobody has to chase anybody. Would that be appropriate?

entries.trigger_signal: prospect says they're too busy right now and asks you to call them back, or otherwise won't commit to keep talking

entries.title: Principles for handling early-stage stalls
entries.summary: How to defuse 'send me info / call me back' stalls without conceding the sale or wasting time.

points: Agree first, then reframe. Adding a line like 'you might not even need us' disarms the prospect and lowers their guard so they'll answer your questions.
Never send a proposal or information until you've confirmed the person is serious about changing their situation - otherwise you burn selling time on someone who ghosts you.
Ask for THEIR timeframe to get back to you, not the other way around. It positions you as the busy expert whose time is valuable rather than a salesperson they can shrug off.
Book a concrete calendar time instead of accepting a vague 'I'll call you back' - it ends the chase and frames you as an authority.
If a booked callback is missed, wait a couple of minutes before reaching out so it doesn't look like you were waiting by the phone.

entries.trigger_signal: any early-stage stall objection is detected before a gap has been built

entries.title: Ask an existing customer for referrals
entries.summary: After you've delivered value, get the customer to articulate how you helped (so they own it), then guide them to name people they know with the same problem and help them plan the introduction.

questions: I appreciate the chance to work with you. Can I ask - in your own words, where do you feel we've helped you the most?
With that in mind, who do you know who might be wrestling with the same problem we solved for you?
Can you tell me a bit more about them, and why you feel I might be able to help them?
How do you think would be the best way to reach out to them?
Do you feel it'd be worth letting them know first that I'll be getting in touch?
What do you think you'd want to say to them?
Could I offer a suggestion? What if you mentioned the challenges you'd been dealing with, that they're facing something similar, and how we helped you with it - would that land better with them?
So aside from that person, who else do you feel we might be able to help?

entries.trigger_signal: stage=commit AND value has been delivered or the deal is won; rep is opening the referral ask with a served customer

entries.title: Open a call or meeting with a referred prospect
entries.summary: How to start the first contact with someone who was referred - naming the mutual connection and the problem you solved, then handing control to the prospect rather than assuming interest.

questions: Hi, is this the right person? This is your name. A mutual contact of ours suggested I reach out - I recently helped them with a problem that was causing them some trouble, and they mentioned you might be running into something similar. Is now an okay time to talk?

Great to meet you. So I don't repeat things you've already gone over with our mutual contact, would you mind sharing what the two of you discussed, and then what you'd like to focus on today, so we can center this on you and what you might be looking for?

entries.trigger_signal: stage=connect AND the lead originated from a referral or warm introduction

entries.title: Referral best-practices
entries.summary: Mindset and language rules that keep referral asks and referral calls from triggering resistance.

points: Don't lead with yourself or your company. Make the ask about the customer and how they feel you've helped them so they own the value and want to introduce you.
Never assume a referral is automatically interested just because someone passed their name along - your first job is still to uncover whether they even have a problem worth solving.
Let go of the outcome and focus on whether you can actually help. Problem-finders and problem-solvers earn trust; product-pushers get price-shopped and ghosted.
Use tentative, neutral language like 'might be' when describing the referral's possible problems - stating it as fact triggers resistance and makes assertive personalities push back and deny it.
Drop pressure phrases like 'so you can make an informed decision' or 'we don't just work with anyone' - they manufacture sales pressure even on a warm referral.

entries.trigger_signal: rep is about to ask for a referral or make first contact with a referred prospect

entries.title: Tone on stalls, openers, and referral calls
entries.summary: Delivery guidance: the tone at the start of a call drives resistance more than the words.

points: The tone you use at the very start of a call causes more sales resistance than the words themselves - an eager, pushy delivery makes prospects stall and pile on objections.
Deliver stall-handling and referral questions calmly, curiously, and unhurried so the prospect's guard stays down.
When calling a referral, don't sound excited or assumptive; a relaxed, problem-focused tone keeps them from getting defensive.

entries.trigger_signal: start of a call OR while handling a stall or referral; detect an eager/pushy tone or fast pace

entries.title: De-escalate and resolve an upset customer
entries.summary: When an existing customer complains, ask questions to understand and to make them feel heard instead of arguing the facts - the goal is to win the relationship, not the argument.

questions: Just so I understand - what exactly happened?
Can you walk me through that in a bit more detail?
Thanks for flagging this. Can you tell me everything you know about what happened, and how the other side has reacted so far?
What else can you tell me about the situation?
How do you think things got to this point?
I'm sorry this happened. What would you like to see done so we can put it right for you?
This bothers me too - how soon can we meet in person to talk it through?
Would it help if I dug into the facts and then we regrouped to go over some possible ways to fix this?
If anything else comes up in the meantime, will you bring it straight to me so I can help?

entries.trigger_signal: an existing customer raises a complaint or is upset about the product/service

entries.title: Monitor account health to keep customers
entries.summary: Periodic relationship-monitoring questions for existing clients; the answers reveal whether the relationship is strong or at risk and open the door to improvements and expansion.

questions: Where do you feel we're helping you most, and why? What changes could we make to get you even bigger results?
What goals would you like us to help you reach over the next quarter or year?
How do you see us being different from the vendor you used before - and why do you feel that way?
How could we make your life easier? Tell me more...
In what ways do you think we could improve to make things better on your end?
Would you be open to giving me some advice on how we could do better for you?
What do you feel we're doing best for you - the thing that's really helping you get where you want to go?

entries.trigger_signal: post-sale check-in or account review with an existing customer
